Push
PUUSH
v.t.
From Old French poulser, to thrust, from Latin pulsare, to beat or strike. Webster 1828: to press against with force; to drive by pressure. In Scripture it is a horn word — the action of a goring ox, and by extension the conquest of a nation.

Biblical Definition

The Hebrew verb belongs first to livestock, and the law is exact about the liability: If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned (Exodus 21:32). The sum is worth remembering — thirty pieces of silver, the price the law set on a slave gored by a beast, and the price at which the Son of God was sold. From the ox the figure passes to the nation. Moses blesses Joseph with horns: his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 33:17). Daniel sees the Medo-Persian empire in exactly this posture: I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; so that no beasts might stand before him... but he did according to his will, and became great (Daniel 8:4) — and the following verses bring the he-goat that breaks him, for the ram’s own will is not the last word. The word is also the vehicle of false prophecy: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them (1 Kings 22:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PUSH as to press against with force; to drive or impel by pressure; to thrust, as with a pointed instrument or with the horns, as an ox.

expand to see more

PUSH, v.t. — To press against with force; to drive or impel by pressure.

To butt; to thrust with the horns or with a pointed instrument; as, an ox pushes with his horns.

To press or urge forward; as, to push an objection too far.

PUSH, n. — A thrust; a pressure; an assault or attack; an effort.

Old French poulser, from Latin pulsare, to beat — the root also of pulse and repulse.

Key Scripture

Exodus 21:32 — "If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned."

Deuteronomy 33:17 — "His glory is like the firstling of his bullock, and his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh."

Daniel 8:4 — "I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; so that no beasts might stand before him, neither was there any that could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and became great."

1 Kings 22:11 — "And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them."

Modern Corruption

Zedekiah’s iron horns are the model of confident false prophecy — a dramatic sign, the formula Thus saith the LORD, four hundred agreeing voices, and a message that was simply untrue.

expand to see more

1 Kings 22 is the fullest case study of false prophecy in the Old Testament, and every mark of it is present. Zedekiah has a visual aid, the correct formula (Thus saith the LORD), overwhelming numerical support, and a message the king wanted. Micaiah has none of these and is imprisoned for saying so. The chapter is decisive against the assumption that consensus, sincerity or spiritual impressiveness authenticate a word from God; the only test Scripture gives is agreement with what God has already spoken, and the outcome in Deuteronomy 18:22. This is why the dictionary is cessationist and holds the canon closed. Modern prophetic ministries that issue predictions, revise them, and continue without repentance are operating in Zedekiah’s line, and the fact that some of them are warm and evidently sincere is exactly what the chapter warns will be the case.

Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels of silver as the compensation for a slave gored by an ox, and Zechariah 11:12-13 has the LORD Himself appraised at that goodly price, and Matthew 26:15 records the bargain struck. Scripture is deliberate about this figure. It is not a coincidence to be admired but a valuation to be felt: the priests of Israel priced the Son of God at the statutory rate for damaged property. The typology runs through the law rather than around it, which is a standing argument against the habit of treating the Mosaic case laws as culturally expired curiosities. They are the vocabulary in which the New Testament states the worth of Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nagach (H5055), to butt or gore with the horn; qeren (H7161), a horn; Greek keratizo, to gore; the ram of Daniel 8 is Aramaic-era Hebrew ayil (H352).

expand to see more

Hebrew nagach (H5055) — to gore or push with the horn; used of the ox (Exodus 21:32), Joseph (Deuteronomy 33:17) and the ram (Daniel 8:4).

Hebrew qeren (H7161) — a horn, the standing biblical figure for strength and dominion.

Hebrew reem (H7214) — the wild ox, rendered unicorn in the Authorized Version (Deuteronomy 33:17).

Hebrew ayil (H352) — a ram; the Medo-Persian empire in Daniel’s vision (Daniel 8:4, 8:20).

Hebrew sheqel (H8255) — the shekel; thirty of them the price of a gored servant (Exodus 21:32).

Usage

"If the ox shall push a manservant... thirty shekels of silver (Exodus 21:32) — the statutory price the priests later set on Christ."

"With them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth (Deuteronomy 33:17) — the horn as the figure of dominion."

"With these shalt thou push the Syrians (1 Kings 22:11) — a dramatic sign, the right formula, and a false word."
